text_a:
Alexia Amesbury (born c. 1951, née Jumeau) is a Seychellois politician and a lawyer by profession. Under the umbrella of the Seychelles Party for Social Justice and Democracy, she contested in the 2015 presidential election to become the first woman to contest a Seychellois presidential election.

Early life 
***
Amesbury was born at Praslin, Mahé, Seychelles and grew up in the St. Elizabeth's Convent in Seychelles until she moved to Kenya in 1961 where she completed her O' and A'levels.

Education
***
At the age of 37, she matriculated at a University in the United Kingdom to study Law before proceeding to the London School of Economics and Political Science where a master's degree in International Law.

Career
***
In 2015, she became the first woman to contest in a Seychellois presidential election after she represented the Seychelles Party for Social Justice and Democracy during the 2015 presidential election. She received a total of 803 votes in the first round. While Amesbury did not advance to the second round of voting, she supported Wavel Ramkalawan in the run-off election.

Controversy
***
After James Michel won the 2015 election, Amesbury believed that the results were invalid based on Seychelles's Constitution. Amesbury explained that according to the Constitution of Seychelles, the fifth section of Schedule 3 states that a candidate in Seychelles cannot be elected president unless they receive more than half of the votes during the election.

Personal life 
***
In 1972, she married an Englishman with whom she had six children. The couple divorced in 1998.

title_a: OUR LA DIGUE CAMPAIGN WAS A HUGE SUCCESS!
text_a:
🇸🇨🐾 349 CATS AND DOGS STERILIZED 🐶🐱❤️

After six intense surgery days, countless hours of cat trapping, torrential tropical rainstorms and a few unexpected challenges, our Network for Animals veterinary team has completed its second sterilization campaign on La Digue Island in the Seychelles!

And what an incredible achievement:

❤️ 349 cats and dogs sterilized
🐶 84 dogs – 45 females and 39 males
🐱 265 cats – 138 females and 127 males

🐾 202 unowned community and feral cats were humanely trapped, sterilized and returned to their familiar surroundings – representing an incredible 76% of all cats sterilized during the campaign.

Every sterilization means fewer unwanted litters, fewer vulnerable puppies and kittens born into hardship, and a brighter future for La Digue's cats and dogs.

It wasn't easy. Torrential rain severely disrupted our trapping operations, made it difficult for owners to bring their animals to the clinic and complicated efforts to catch roaming dogs. Several team members also suffered infected cat bites that required hospital treatment.

But our team persevered, working tirelessly to help as many animals as possible.

And the impact is already visible. On our final morning on La Digue, one of our team members spotted seven cats during a bicycle ride. Six had ear tips – a sign that they had already been sterilized ❤️

None of this would have been possible without our incredible supporters, our dedicated veterinary and trapping teams, our campaign partners Seychelles SPCA and Be Kind, and the wonderful La Digue community who welcomed us back with open arms.

THANK YOU for helping us tackle pet overpopulation, prevent suffering and create a future with fewer homeless cats and dogs on La Digue 🇸🇨❤️!

On the visit of the Russian Navy frigate "Marshal Shaposhnikov" to the port of Victoria

From November 1 to 5, the Russian Navy frigate "Marshal Shaposhnikov" is making a port call at Victoria, Republic of Seychelles. This third visit by Russian naval vessels to the territorial waters of Seychelles this year is new evidence of the successful development of mutually beneficial bilateral cooperation in various fields, including maritime security.

Joint exercises conducted by the crew of the "Marshal Shaposhnikov" and the Seychelles Defence Forces on November 5 are dedicated to strengthening maritime security. The visit of the Russian ship takes place in an atmosphere of friendship and openness inherent to Russian-Seychellois relations throughout their half-century history, while the first visit of a Russian Navy ship dates back to the 19th century. 

On November 2, the commander of the deployment, Rear Admiral Evgeny Myasoedov, and Chargé d'Affaires of the Russian Federation to the Republic of Seychelles, Mr. Dmitrii Iordanidi, met with the Deputy Chief of the Seychelles Defence Forces, Brigadier General Jean Attala. An engaging conversation was held on the further development of maritime cooperation between Moscow and Victoria, as well as Russia's assistance in training personnel for the Seychellois maritime sector. On the same day, a wreath-laying ceremony took place at the grave of Alexander Krupenin, the ship's doctor of the cruiser "Razboynik," who passed away while the vessel was in Indian Ocean waters in 1895 and was buried in Seychelles.

On November 3, a reception was held aboard the frigate "Marshal Shaposhnikov" in a warm, cordial atmosphere ahead of National Unity Day celebrated in Russia. The event was attended by VIP guests, including the Vice President of the Republic of Seychelles, Mr. Sebastien Pillay, the Deputy Chief of the Seychelles Defence Forces, Brigadier General Jean Attala Attala, as well as heads of ministries and agencies, ambassadors, heads of diplomatic missions, and other officials. The guests highly praised the performance of musicians from the Pacific Fleet Song and Dance Ensemble, which accompanied the event.

During the stay of the "Marshal Shaposhnikov" in Victoria, crew representatives visited the Seychelles Maritime Academy and participated in a friendly football match with service members of the Seychelles Defence Forces.

On November 4, citizens of Seychelles, including schoolchildren, foreign guests of the archipelago, and compatriots, went on a guided tour of the ship to get a closer look at the service of Russian sailors.

text_a:
President Herminie visits STC, sets vision for a new Seychelles Trading Company by 2030

President Dr. Patrick Herminie today visited the Seychelles Trading Company (STC), marking the first time a President has toured the company's facilities, in several years. The visit follows his announcement that he will personally lead the STC portfolio, as part of his commitment to bring down the cost of living for Seychellois families.

The President was accompanied by the Minister for Finance, Economic Planning, Trade and Investment, Mr Pierre Laporte, and the Chairperson of the STC Board, Mrs Lekha Nair. He was welcomed by the company's new management team, led by Chief Executive Ms Iouana Pillay and Deputy Chief Executive Mr Ronny Brutus.

During his tour of the sorting facility, the bakery, the Gift Shop area and several warehouses, the President met staff and saw the company's day-to-day operations first-hand. The management briefed him on its plans to make STC the leading and most competitive trader in Seychelles, while keeping the prices of essential commodities low and safeguarding national food security.

Discussions also focused on the company's ageing infrastructure, with much of its equipment and facilities more than 25 years old. The President stressed the importance of preventive maintenance, noting that regular upkeep extends the life of equipment, avoids costly breakdowns and keeps essential goods moving without disruption. In turn, the management outlined its plans to modernise and digitalise STC's services, invest in new areas of business and expand its market to the hotel sector.

Speaking to the media after the visit, President Herminie said he wants to see a new STC by 2030, and he expressed his full support for the new management. He reiterated that STC's core mandate is to anchor prices, adding that he will do everything in his power to bring down the cost of living and give citizens better value for money.

The President also encouraged the management to look beyond Seychelles and learn from the experience of other countries in the region and across the African continent.

📅 24 OCTOBER | THIS DAY IN AFRICAN HISTORY

🇿🇲 1964: ZAMBIA CELEBRATES ITS INDEPENDENCE

On 24 October 1964, Zambia gained independence from British colonial rule.

Previously known as Northern Rhodesia, the country became an independent republic, with Kenneth Kaunda as its first president.

But Zambia’s independence was important far beyond its borders.

Under Kaunda, the country became a centre of support for liberation movements fighting colonial and white minority rule across southern Africa.

Movements from South Africa, Zimbabwe, Namibia and other countries received political support and refuge in Zambia.

This came at a considerable cost, as Zambia faced economic and security pressures because of its position.

Kaunda’s domestic political record was more complicated, particularly after Zambia became a one-party state.

Nevertheless, Zambia’s contribution to the liberation of southern Africa remains an important part of its history.

Today marks 62 years of Zambian independence.

Happy Independence Day to the people of Zambia!

🇪🇬 1973: THE PEOPLE OF SUEZ RESISTED DURING THE OCTOBER WAR

On 24 October 1973, Egyptian civilians and security forces resisted Israeli troops during the October War.

The fighting took place around Suez, an Egyptian city near the southern end of the Suez Canal.

The October War had begun on 6 October, when Egyptian and Syrian forces launched attacks against Israeli positions.

By 24 October, despite international efforts to establish a ceasefire, fighting continued around Suez.

Egyptian resistance fighters, supported by soldiers and police, confronted Israeli forces attempting to take control of the city.

Their resistance became an important symbol of Egyptian determination.

Today, Suez Governorate commemorates 24 October as its National Day.

The anniversary honours those who defended the city during one of the most significant conflicts in modern Egyptian history.

Today marks 53 years since that resistance.

🇰🇪 2018: ELIUD KIPCHOGE RECEIVED A UNITED NATIONS AWARD

On 24 October 2018, Kenyan marathon champion Eliud Kipchoge was honoured as the United Nations in Kenya Person of the Year.

The award recognised more than his achievements in athletics.

Just weeks earlier, Kipchoge had broken the men’s marathon world record at the Berlin Marathon, completing the race in 2 hours, 1 minute and 39 seconds.

But the United Nations also recognised his commitment to inspiring young people and supporting efforts to address HIV/AIDS in Kenya.

Kipchoge had become an international symbol of discipline, perseverance and determination.

His message was that extraordinary achievements come through years of consistent effort.

The award was presented during celebrations marking United Nations Day in Nairobi.

Today marks eight years since Kipchoge received the honour.

His story reminds us that African sporting excellence can influence lives far beyond the competition itself.

🇸🇨 2020: SEYCHELLES HELD AN ELECTION THAT CHANGED ITS POLITICAL HISTORY

On 24 October 2020, voting concluded in a historic presidential and parliamentary election in Seychelles.

Seychelles is an island nation in the Indian Ocean, off the eastern coast of Africa.

Since 1977, the country’s presidency had remained in the hands of the same political movement.

But the election of October 2020 brought a remarkable change.

The following day, election officials announced that opposition candidate Wavel Ramkalawan had won the presidency with approximately 54.9% of the vote.

He defeated incumbent President Danny Faure.

It was the first time an opposition candidate had won the presidency since Seychelles gained independence in 1976.

The opposition also secured a substantial parliamentary majority.

The election demonstrated that political power could change hands through the ballot box.

Today marks six years since voting concluded in that historic election.

It remains an important chapter in the democratic history of this African island nation.

🌍 TODAY’S REFLECTION

Today’s stories celebrate different forms of African courage and achievement.

Zambia’s independence strengthened the wider struggle for African liberation.

The people of Suez demonstrated resistance during a difficult period of war.

Eliud Kipchoge showed how sporting excellence can inspire future generations.

And voters in Seychelles demonstrated the power of democratic participation.

Which of these stories do you believe deserves greater recognition in African history, and why?

In ten days, it will be three months since Justice Antony Fernando retired as President of the Court of Appeal. That a position of such constitutional importance remains unfilled nearly three months later should concern every Seychellois who believes in the independence of the judiciary and the integrity of public institutions.

According to information obtained by LSH, an impasse has emerged between State House and the Constitutional Appointment Authority (CAA) over the appointment of a successor. Two women were reportedly proposed: an expatriate judge and a Seychellois judge. President Patrick Herminie is understood to be opposed to the local nominee, while the Ghanaian candidate has since taken up another position.

The circumstances surrounding the delay remain unclear. But that uncertainty is precisely the problem.

Appointments to the highest levels of the judiciary should never become a source of political speculation. Nor should the public be left to wonder whether constitutional processes are being stalled by disagreement, personal preference or political calculation. The credibility of the judiciary depends not only on the quality of its judges but also on the integrity and transparency of the processes through which they are appointed.

The President and the relevant constitutional authorities owe the public a clear explanation. If there are legitimate reasons for the delay, they should be communicated. If disagreements have arisen over the nominees, the constitutional mechanisms for resolving them should be respected.

A constitutional office cannot be treated as an administrative inconvenience, much less a political bargaining chip. The longer this vacancy persists without explanation, the greater the risk that public confidence will be eroded.

For the United Seychelles administration, this is an opportunity to demonstrate that constitutional governance is more than a promise made during elections. It is a responsibility exercised in public, according to established rules and without fear or favour.

Silence may conceal the reasons for the delay, but it cannot indefinitely dispel the suspicion it creates. Seychelles deserves better.

𝗕𝘆 Gilbert J Pool - 𝗚𝗣𝗦 𝗦𝗲𝘆𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗲𝘀

𝗜𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁, 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗲𝘆𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗼𝗶𝘀 𝗦𝗼𝘂𝗹: 𝒘𝒉𝒚 𝒘𝒆 𝒎𝒖𝒔𝒕 𝒎𝒐𝒗𝒆 𝒘𝒊𝒕𝒉 𝒄𝒂𝒓𝒆

Mahé, our main island, has very little flat land, and most of it is already used for homes, farms, hotels and offices.

Yet this morning in the National Assembly, members were asking who might next buy what little remains.

𝑾𝒉𝒂𝒕 𝒘𝒂𝒔 𝒔𝒂𝒊𝒅 𝒊𝒏 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝑨𝒔𝒔𝒆𝒎𝒃𝒍𝒚

Members questioned Vice President Sebastien Pillay about the Principal Minister, Wallace Cosgrow, and his recent visit to Zurich. He attended a high-level, exclusive meeting convened by Henley & Partners, a London-based firm that advises governments on the design and operation of residence and citizenship by investment programmes.

The question was simple. Was the visit about attracting foreign direct investment (FDI), meaning money from abroad put into local businesses and projects? Or did it signal a return to selling Seychellois passports?

The Vice President stressed that our economy needs FDI, both for its own sake and to encourage more local investment.

He also made clear that any special programme would need the endorsement of the National Assembly.

It is worth saying plainly that attending a meeting is not a decision, and nothing here points to wrongdoing.

Members asked fair questions, and the Vice President gave fair answers. The value of this moment is that it invites us to think before anything is proposed, not after.

𝑻𝒉𝒆 𝒏𝒆𝒆𝒅 𝒊𝒔 𝒓𝒆𝒂𝒍

We are a small island economy that depends heavily on tourism and fishing and badly needs locally-grown food.

Our young people want good jobs, and our businesses want partners and capital. Turning away every outside investor would not protect us. It would leave us poorer and more dependent on a few sectors.

So the real question is not whether we welcome investment. It is what kind, on what terms, and with what safeguards.

𝑾𝒉𝒚 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒍𝒂𝒏𝒅 𝒒𝒖𝒆𝒔𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏 𝒊𝒔 𝒔𝒆𝒏𝒔𝒊𝒕𝒊𝒗𝒆

Members voiced a specific worry. They fear that unethical investors might go on a property buying spree, as has happened before, leaving Seychellois with fewer chances to own land.

This is not an imagined fear. In 2013, then-President James Michel announced plans to stop non-Seychellois from buying state land on a freehold basis.

In 2014 the government adjusted the policy, allowing non-Seychellois to buy privately owned land only, subject to set criteria and government sanction.

The same reporting noted that some foreigners had used nominee companies with Seychellois majority shareholders to get around the rules.

It also observed that land for building homes is scarce, and that speculation by foreign buyers had helped push up property prices.

In other words, we have been here before. The rules that exist were written because of real experience, and any new scheme should be tested against them.

𝑴𝒐𝒓𝒆 𝒕𝒉𝒂𝒏 𝒎𝒐𝒏𝒆𝒚 𝒊𝒔 𝒂𝒕 𝒔𝒕𝒂𝒌𝒆

Land is not only a commercial asset in Seychelles. It is where families grow up, where a son builds beside his parents, and where a young couple hopes to settle.

When prices climb beyond ordinary reach, something is lost that no investment figure can measure.

The environment carries the same weight. Our beaches, forests, wetlands and coastlines are what visitors come for, and they are also what make this place home. Once a hillside is cleared or a shoreline built over, we cannot easily undo it.

𝑨 𝒄𝒂𝒓𝒆𝒇𝒖𝒍 𝒘𝒂𝒚 𝒇𝒐𝒓𝒘𝒂𝒓𝒅

If the government ever brings a special investment programme to the Assembly, several safeguards would help build public trust:

Publish the purpose early. Citizens should hear what is being considered, and why, before decisions are made.

Debate it openly. The Assembly's endorsement, as the Vice President rightly noted, should follow real scrutiny and public consultation, not a rushed vote.

Protect land for Seychellois. Clear limits on what investors may buy, and where, would keep housing and family plots within reach.

Set environmental red lines. Sensitive coastlines, wetlands and forests should be off the table, whatever the price offered.

Check who is investing. Independent, thorough background checks on the source of funds and the people behind them are essential for a small country with limited resources to police abuse.

Report the results. Regular, public reporting on what came in, where it went and who benefited would keep everyone honest.

𝑲𝒆𝒆𝒑𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒐𝒖𝒓 𝒃𝒂𝒍𝒂𝒏𝒄𝒆

Small islands do not get many second chances. A decision made in haste can be felt for generations, while a decision made carefully can serve us for just as long.

Seychelles can welcome investment and still guard its land, its nature and its character. That balance is not easy to hold, but it is worth the effort.

The best time to insist on transparency is at the very beginning, while the conversation is still open.

**Wavel Ramkalawan – Part 1: When the Questions Get Difficult**

Watching Wavel Ramkalawan being questioned before the CCCL Commission raises some very basic questions.

**Ted Barbe was appointed Commissioner of Police by Wavel Ramkalawan in 2021. Wavel described him as the “best candidate” and publicly gave him his full support.**

And in 2022, Wavel publicly congratulated Barbe for the leadership he was showing and said he was confident the police would do what they needed to do.

**So here is what I find interesting.**

**If there were serious problems with how the police were handling matters while Barbe was Commissioner, why was he given the opportunity to explain himself publicly?**

**Why was the Commissioner not regularly brought before the public to answer questions about the issues under his responsibility?**

**And what about the Minister responsible for Internal Affairs?**

**In fact, after the 7 December 2023 explosion, "Wavel himself held a live press conference and said he would answer questions from the local media."**

So I have to ask:

**Why did Wavel personally take on that responsibility?**

**Was it because he was ultimately taking responsibility for what was happening under his administration? **

**Was it because he trusted his Commissioner and Minister to handle their responsibilities? Or was there simply a different understanding at the time of who should answer for what?**

**These are fair questions.**

Because now, listening to the evidence before the Commission, we are hearing questions about things that Barbe allegedly did — or failed to do — while he was Commissioner.

**But if those failures were happening at the time, **who knew about them? When did they know? And what did they do about them?****

**if Barbe ultimately failed in his responsibilities, let the evidence establish that.**

**But surely political accountability also means asking whether the people who appointed and oversaw the system recognised those failures and acted on them while they were happening.**

It is about following the chain of responsibility.

**Who knew what? When did they know it? Who was supposed to act? And why wasn't it dealt with at the time?**

The Commission is there to ask difficult questions.

And sometimes the difficult questions are not only for the person being investigated.

**They are for everyone who had responsibility at the time.**

title_a: Giant tortoises are thriving: about 180,000 estimated on Aldabra
text_a:
Giant tortoises are thriving: a new study estimates about 180,000 live on Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles.

Aldabra is a ring of coral islands in the Indian Ocean and home to the largest free-roaming giant tortoise population in the world. The survey, led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation and the University of Exeter, analysed five years of tortoise counts from 2018 to 2022. It produced an estimate of approximately 180,000 tortoises, the highest figure ever recorded for the species. The study, published in Ecology and Evolution, found the population relatively stable.

In the 19th century, heavy exploitation left fewer than 1,000 tortoises on Aldabra. Since then the atoll has been protected, as a strict nature reserve since 1981 and a UNESCO site since 1982. The researchers say the new figure is a baseline for tracking the population in the future. Threats remain: longer and more frequent droughts, rising sea levels, and feral cats and black rats that prey on eggs and hatchlings.

Key facts:
• About 180,000 giant tortoises are estimated to live on Aldabra, an atoll in the Seychelles.
• It is the largest free-roaming giant tortoise population in the world.
• The once-endangered species is now described as thriving.
• Aldabra has been a strict nature reserve since 1981 and a UNESCO site since 1982.

More than one billion tonnes of food are wasted worldwide each year, even as an estimated 645 million people experienced hunger in 2025, according to figures highlighted in an Al Jazeera report published on World Food Day, October 16, 2026.
The UN Environment Programme estimates that 1.05 billion tonnes of food were wasted by households, restaurants and retailers in 2022. Households accounted for 60% of the total, followed by food services at 28% and retailers at 12%.
🌍 Which countries waste the most food?
UN estimates cited by Al Jazeera put the Maldives at the top, with approximately 260kg of food wasted per person annually. Syria, the Dominican Republic, Seychelles, Mexico and Tunisia were also among the countries with high per-capita food waste.
Meanwhile, Africa had approximately 309 million undernourished people in 2025 — around one in five people on the continent.
🏠 How to reduce food waste
Plan meals and shop with a list.
Store food correctly and freeze items before they spoil.
Cook appropriate portions.
Use leftovers safely.
Eat older food before newly purchased items.
Compost suitable food scraps.
Food loss and waste cost the global economy more than $1 trillion annually and contribute to greenhouse gas emissions. Reducing waste can help households save money while conserving resources and protecting the environment.

text_a:
More than 180,000 giant tortoises now roam a remote island paradise in the Indian Ocean. Their ancestors came dangerously close to extinction, but decades of conservation have helped turn their survival into one of the most remarkable wildlife recovery stories in the world.

Located in the Seychelles, Aldabra Atoll is home to the world's largest free-roaming population of giant tortoises. These enormous reptiles, scientifically known as Aldabrachelys gigantea, are among the last surviving giant tortoise populations on Earth.

Their history, however, was not always so promising. During the 18th and 19th centuries, sailors and traders heavily exploited giant tortoises for food, often collecting them in large numbers and transporting them aboard ships. By the end of the 19th century, hunting had reduced Aldabra's population to fewer than 1,000 individuals.

Fortunately, stronger conservation measures helped protect the remaining animals and their habitat. Aldabra received strict nature reserve protection in 1981 and was recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.

In October 2026, researchers from the University of Exeter and the Seychelles Islands Foundation announced a new scientific estimate of approximately 182,424 adult and sub-adult tortoises. The research analyzed years of population monitoring data collected between 2018 and 2022.

Interestingly, scientists explained that earlier estimates had probably missed many tortoises hiding in dense vegetation. This means the new figure does not represent a sudden population explosion, but rather a more accurate assessment of how many animals actually live there.

Beyond their impressive numbers, these ancient reptiles play an essential role in their ecosystem. They graze on vegetation, disperse seeds, and influence the growth of plants across the islands, helping maintain the natural balance of their habitat.

Despite their recovery, climate change, prolonged droughts, rising sea levels, and invasive predators continue to threaten their long-term survival.

Aldabra's giant tortoises demonstrate how sustained conservation and scientific monitoring can protect wildlife for generations.

title_a: President Herminie Opens Bon Espoir High Security Prison, Strengthening Seychelles’ Correctional System
text_a:
President Herminie Opens Bon Espoir High Security Prison, Strengthening Seychelles’ Correctional System

Strengthening prison security while keeping rehabilitation and human dignity at the core of Seychelles’ correctional system was the key theme highlighted during the official opening of the Bon Espoir High Security Prison attended by President Dr Patrick Herminie today.

The new facility represents an important step towards improving Seychelles’ correctional system, allowing for better management of high-risk inmates, easing pressure on existing prisons and creating a more secure and effective environment for rehabilitation.

Built at SCR 21.41 million, the facility has an initial capacity of 21 inmates. A second phase is also envisaged, with plans to double its capacity

The ceremony was attended by Cabinet Ministers, senior government officials and officers of the Seychelles Prison Service.

Addressing the gathering, the Principal Secretary for Homeland Security, Ms Michelle Sabury, emphasised that correctional institutions must go beyond secure custody by providing opportunities for rehabilitation and reintegration into society.

She also highlighted the importance of supporting prison officers with the necessary resources, professional development and appropriate working conditions.

The Commissioner of Prisons, Mr Antoine Denousse, also addressed the ceremony, emphasising that security and rehabilitation are complementary responsibilities.

Commissioner Denousse said, “The facility is an important investment in national security and the administration of justice. I would also like to take this opportunity to recognise the dedication of prison officers and the contributions of those involved in the project's development.”

President Herminie marked the official opening with the unveiling of a commemorative plaque, followed by a guided tour of the facility.

The prison is expected to begin receiving inmates between December 2026 and January 2027, subject to the completion of staffing and operational arrangements.

To strengthen its workforce, the Seychelles Prison Service is undertaking the recruitment of foreign prison officers following the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding with the Tanzania Prisons Service.

L'autorità antiriciclaggio americana FinCEN ha designato l'exchange MEXC Global come istituto di „primaria preoccupazione per riciclaggio". Le banche statunitensi non potranno più gestire trasferimenti che coinvolgono MEXC. La misura entrerà in vigore 30 giorni dopo la pubblicazione nella Gazzetta ufficiale.

Secondo FinCEN, l'exchange con sede alle Seychelles ha gestito tra il 2021 e il 2026 almeno 16 miliardi di dollari di transazioni illecite. text_b:
Significant enforcement action establishing the Seychelles-based MEXC Global as a jurisdiction of primary money laundering concern for which funds transmittal is now prohibited. 

This is another major FinCEN action taken as part of Operation Economic Outcast that has a major Russia focus, with the other recent action being the proposed rule to prohibit funds transmittal to the A7 Network and its sub-agents. 

Call me curious why FinCEN chose to proceed by order against MEXC Global while opting for a proposed rule against the A7 Network's sub-agents. Both actions rely on the same statutory authority, which expressly permits either approach. Why the difference in urgency? Most likely explanation is the fact that the A7 Network is so well integrated into traditional financial channels that an immediate order would have been too disruptive. 

--

Per @USTreasury: "MEXC Global is a convertible virtual currency (CVC) exchanger that has facilitated at least $16 billion in illicit transactions connected to Iranian, North Korean, and Russian sanctions evasion, as well as cybercrime, including by transacting directly with sanctioned actors."

title_a: Seychelles Island Now Has 183,000 Giant Tortoises — More Than the Country's Entire Population
text_a:
A new study led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation and the University of Exeter has revealed that Aldabra Atoll in Seychelles is home to approximately 183,000 adult and sub-adult Aldabra giant tortoises, the largest known population of free-roaming giant tortoises in the world. 

The findings, published in the journal Ecology and Evolution, mark the first rigorous atoll-wide estimate since the widely cited figure of 100,000 from the late 1990s.

Researchers analysed five years of tortoise counts collected between 2018 and 2022 and used a statistical modelling technique to account for animals hidden in dense scrub and other hard-to-survey habitats. 

The estimate exceeds the Seychelles human population, recorded at 123,565 by the National Bureau of Statistics as of June 2026.

In the 19th century, exploitation reduced the Aldabra giant tortoise population to fewer than 1,000 individuals. 

Aldabra became a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982, after which the population gradually recovered. 

Despite the positive numbers, the study's authors caution that longer and more frequent droughts are expected to reduce food and shade, rising sea levels threaten low-lying areas of the atoll, and invasive feral cats and black rats continue to prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings.

text_a:
More than 180,000 giant tortoises now roam a remote island paradise in the Indian Ocean. Their ancestors came dangerously close to extinction, but decades of conservation have helped turn their survival into one of the most remarkable wildlife recovery stories in the world.

Located in the Seychelles, Aldabra Atoll is home to the world's largest free-roaming population of giant tortoises. These enormous reptiles, scientifically known as Aldabrachelys gigantea, are among the last surviving giant tortoise populations on Earth.

Their history, however, was not always so promising. During the 18th and 19th centuries, sailors and traders heavily exploited giant tortoises for food, often collecting them in large numbers and transporting them aboard ships. By the end of the 19th century, hunting had reduced Aldabra's population to fewer than 1,000 individuals.

Fortunately, stronger conservation measures helped protect the remaining animals and their habitat. Aldabra received strict nature reserve protection in 1981 and was recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.

In October 2026, researchers from the University of Exeter and the Seychelles Islands Foundation announced a new scientific estimate of approximately 182,424 adult and sub-adult tortoises. The research analyzed years of population monitoring data collected between 2018 and 2022.

Interestingly, scientists explained that earlier estimates had probably missed many tortoises hiding in dense vegetation. This means the new figure does not represent a sudden population explosion, but rather a more accurate assessment of how many animals actually live there.

Beyond their impressive numbers, these ancient reptiles play an essential role in their ecosystem. They graze on vegetation, disperse seeds, and influence the growth of plants across the islands, helping maintain the natural balance of their habitat.

Despite their recovery, climate change, prolonged droughts, rising sea levels, and invasive predators continue to threaten their long-term survival.

Aldabra's giant tortoises demonstrate how sustained conservation and scientific monitoring can protect wildlife for generations.

🚨 A PRESS CONFERENCE IS NOT A SUBSTITUTE FOR PARLIAMENTARY ACCOUNTABILITY.

Questions are mounting over salary adjustments at Air Seychelles, including reported concerns among employees about fairness and transparency.

On 19 October, Opposition Leader Bernard Georges submitted a Private Notice Question (PNQ) seeking answers about management salary reviews and employee dissatisfaction.

The National Assembly sitting on 20 October was cancelled because of adverse weather.

Transport Minister Véronique Laporte subsequently addressed the airline's salary situation through a press conference.

But the central issue remains: Who takes these financial decisions, who approves them, and who is accountable?

⚖️ THE REPUBLIC ASKS:

🔴 1. WHO APPROVES MANAGEMENT SALARIES?

▪️ Does the Air Seychelles Board authorise senior management salary increases?

▪️ What role does the responsible minister play?

▪️ Are salary increases linked to financial performance, responsibilities and transparent criteria?

🔴 2. WHAT ABOUT ORDINARY EMPLOYEES?

▪️ Are pilots, engineers, cabin crew and ground staff receiving fair treatment?

▪️ What consultation took place before salary adjustments were introduced?

▪️ Is there a published timetable for restoring salaries reduced during the pandemic?

🔴 3. WHO ANSWERS TO PARLIAMENT?

▪️ Why should elected representatives have to rely on a press conference for answers to a formal parliamentary question?

▪️ Will the minister provide the financial justification, decision-making process and supporting evidence?

▪️ Will the Air Seychelles Board explain how salary decisions are approved and monitored?

🇸🇨 OUR NATIONAL AIRLINE BELONGS TO THE PEOPLE OF SEYCHELLES.

Air Seychelles needs experienced management, fairly paid employees and a financially sustainable future.

But commercial independence must come with accountability.

Parliament has a responsibility to scrutinise. Ministers have a responsibility to answer. The public has a right to know.

📢 Should salaries and financial decisions at state-owned companies face stronger parliamentary scrutiny?

🇸🇨 THE REPUBLIC SEYCHELLES

Questions matter. Facts matter. Accountability matters.

[ 🌀CYCLONES AUX SEYCHELLES🌀 ]

Bonsoir.

🌀AGUEDA s’affaiblit progressivement⬇️ et ne sera bientôt plus qu’un souvenir. 🌫

☝️Toutefois, son passage direct sur les Seychelles, sous forme de 🌀dépression tropicale, a provoqué des inondations et des dégâts notables. 🌧

🤔Cette situation en a étonné plus d'un!❗️

🧏‍♂️Pourtant, le passage de 🌀cyclones sur l’archipel n’est pas un phénomène inédit : plusieurs épisodes similaires se sont déjà produits par le passé. Le plus récent remonte à la 🌀tempête tropicale de septembre 2002.🌬

☝️Sur ceux, petit retour sur ce 🌀système particulièrement impressionnant, qui a marqué l’histoire des Seychelles.🌩

👉En septembre 2002, une 🌀tempête tropicale precoce a frappé les Seychelles, un archipel rarement exposé aux effets directs des cyclones.🌊

☝️Premier système de la saison 2002/2003, il s’est formé au début du mois de septembre près des îles Chagos. Classé perturbation tropicale le 5 septembre, il est devenu une dépression tropicale le lendemain. ✅️

☝️En progressant vers l’ouest, il s’est rapproché des Seychelles, mais sa menace a d’abord été sous-estimée : ces îles proches de l’équateur étant peu habituées à ce type de phénomène.🤔

➡️Le système s’est toutefois renforcé et a atteint le stade de 🌀tempête tropicale dans l’après-midi du 6 septembre. Désigné sous le numéro 01-2002/2003, il n’a pas reçu de nom en temps réel, ce qui a contribué à une certaine confusion sur sa réelle intensité, tant auprès de la population que des autorités. 🤷‍♂️

Researchers found an island that has a higher population of giant tortoises than people

There are more giant tortoises living on Aldabra Atoll than there are people in the entire country of Seychelles. A new survey estimates that nearly 183,000 tortoises call the atoll home, making it the largest known population of wild giant tortoises.

(📸: Getty)
text_b:
There are more giant tortoises on one Seychelles atoll than there are people in the whole of Seychelles.

A new survey of Aldabra Atoll has counted roughly 180,000 Aldabra giant tortoises roaming free the highest figure ever recorded for the species. The last widely cited number, from the late 1990s, was 100,000.

Aldabra is one of only two places on Earth where giant tortoises still live in the wild. The other is the Galápagos, where the population is much smaller.

In the 19th century, after decades of exploitation, fewer than 1,000 were left on the atoll. A recovery programme followed. Aldabra became a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a UNESCO site the year after, and the tortoises were left alone.

“More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve,” said Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley of the Seychelles Islands Foundation, which led the survey with the University of Exeter.

The count took five years of fieldwork, from 2018 to 2022. Aldabra’s vegetation is dense enough that counting tortoises is genuinely difficult, so the team modelled the ones they couldn’t see as well as the ones they could.

The researchers call it a baseline rather than a finish line. Droughts are getting longer, sea levels are rising on low-lying ground, and feral cats and black rats still take tortoise eggs and hatchlings. Clearing those out, they say, could remove the last thing holding the population back.

title_b: Aldabra Giant Tortoise Species Makes a Comeback🐢
text_b:
The Aldabra giant tortoise is one of the most remarkable examples of wildlife conservation in the Indian Ocean. Native to Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles, these enormous reptiles live in a protected island ecosystem where their grazing, movement, and seed dispersal help shape the surrounding environment.

For centuries, giant tortoises across the Indian Ocean were heavily exploited by sailors and settlers for food. Hunting and habitat changes caused populations on many islands to disappear, leaving Aldabra as one of the last major strongholds for giant tortoises in the region.

Aldabra’s long-term survival was helped by conservation efforts that protected the atoll from extensive development and exploitation. The site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982, recognizing its exceptional natural value and the importance of preserving its unique wildlife.

A scientific study published in 2026 estimated that approximately 180,000 Aldabra giant tortoises live on Aldabra Atoll. Researchers from the Seychelles Islands Foundation and the University of Exeter contributed to the research, which provides a more comprehensive population estimate than earlier surveys. The tortoises now outnumber the human population of the entire Seychelles nation.

The Aldabra giant tortoise, scientifically known as Aldabrachelys gigantea, is one of the world's largest tortoise species. During the 19th century, intensive hunting for meat and other resources devastated giant tortoise populations across the Indian Ocean, leaving Aldabra as their last major natural stronghold in the region.

By the late 1800s, fewer than 1,000 tortoises may have remained on Aldabra. Conservation efforts gradually reduced human exploitation, allowing the population to recover. The atoll's designation as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982 further strengthened protections for its unique ecosystem.

To produce the new estimate, researchers analyzed tortoise monitoring data collected by field teams between 2018 and 2022. Their statistical models accounted for differences in habitat and the likelihood of tortoises being overlooked during surveys. The study appeared in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution.

The new estimate does not necessarily mean the population nearly doubled in recent decades. Earlier surveys estimated around 100,000 tortoises, but researchers believe those methods may have missed animals hidden in dense vegetation or shaded areas. The latest research provides a more reliable picture of a population that appears to have remained relatively stable during the study period.

Aldabra's giant tortoises also play an important ecological role. As large herbivores, they graze on vegetation, create pathways through the landscape, and disperse seeds. These activities help shape the atoll's habitats and influence the other species living there.

Despite their impressive numbers, the tortoises remain vulnerable because their principal wild population is concentrated on one remote atoll. Climate change, rising sea levels, and extreme weather could threaten their habitat in the future. Continued monitoring and conservation management will be important to protect the population.

The discovery demonstrates the value of long-term habitat protection and improved scientific monitoring. Aldabra's giant tortoises have survived centuries of human exploitation, and the latest research shows how sustained conservation can help preserve one of the world's most extraordinary wildlife populations.

Presented by the City Bar's African Affairs Committee, host Justin Loveland, a commercial litigator who previously served as a legal consultant to Seychelles' Truth, Reconciliation and National Unity Commission, is joined by four leading voices in transitional justice who have worked on or alongside truth commissions across the continent: Professor Ron Slye (Kenya and South Africa), the Honorable Bernard Georges (Seychelles), and Didier Gbery and Dr. Baba Jallow (The Gambia).

The panel discusses the legal standards truth commissions rely on and how formal findings differ from narrative truth. Panelists then compare what worked and what didn't in their own countries, from the Gambia's live-broadcast hearings and Kenya's women-only hearings to Seychelles' stalled follow-through, along with challenges like witness protection and cultural silence around sexual violence. The conversation closes on reparations: who should pay, whether perpetrators can be required to compensate victims, how The Gambia delivered interim relief while its commission was still hearing testimony, and why repair may extend well beyond money.

title_a: Seychelles Island Now Has 183,000 Giant Tortoises — More Than the Country's Entire Population
text_a:
A new study led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation and the University of Exeter has revealed that Aldabra Atoll in Seychelles is home to approximately 183,000 adult and sub-adult Aldabra giant tortoises, the largest known population of free-roaming giant tortoises in the world. 

The findings, published in the journal Ecology and Evolution, mark the first rigorous atoll-wide estimate since the widely cited figure of 100,000 from the late 1990s.

Researchers analysed five years of tortoise counts collected between 2018 and 2022 and used a statistical modelling technique to account for animals hidden in dense scrub and other hard-to-survey habitats. 

The estimate exceeds the Seychelles human population, recorded at 123,565 by the National Bureau of Statistics as of June 2026.

In the 19th century, exploitation reduced the Aldabra giant tortoise population to fewer than 1,000 individuals. 

Aldabra became a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982, after which the population gradually recovered. 

Despite the positive numbers, the study's authors caution that longer and more frequent droughts are expected to reduce food and shade, rising sea levels threaten low-lying areas of the atoll, and invasive feral cats and black rats continue to prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings.

From November 1 to 5, the Russian Navy frigate "Marshal Shaposhnikov" is making a port call at Victoria, Republic of Seychelles. This third visit by Russian naval vessels to the territorial waters of Seychelles this year is new evidence of the successful development of mutually beneficial bilateral cooperation in various fields, including maritime security.

Joint exercises conducted by the crew of the "Marshal Shaposhnikov" and the Seychelles Defence Forces on November 5 are dedicated to strengthening maritime security. The visit of the Russian ship takes place in an atmosphere of friendship and openness inherent to Russian-Seychellois relations throughout their half-century history, while the first visit of a Russian Navy ship dates back to the 19th century. 

On November 2, the commander of the deployment, Rear Admiral Evgeny Myasoedov, and Chargé d'Affaires of the Russian Federation to the Republic of Seychelles, Mr. Dmitrii Iordanidi, met with the Deputy Chief of the Seychelles Defence Forces, Brigadier General Jean Attala. An engaging conversation was held on the further development of maritime cooperation between Moscow and Victoria, as well as Russia's assistance in training personnel for the Seychellois maritime sector. On the same day, a wreath-laying ceremony took place at the grave of Alexander Krupenin, the ship's doctor of the cruiser "Razboynik," who passed away while the vessel was in Indian Ocean waters in 1895 and was buried in Seychelles.

On November 3, a reception was held aboard the frigate "Marshal Shaposhnikov" in a warm, cordial atmosphere ahead of National Unity Day celebrated in Russia. During the stay of the "Marshal Shaposhnikov" in Victoria, crew representatives visited the Seychelles Maritime Academy and participated in a friendly football match with service members of the Seychelles Defence Forces.

Aux Seychelles, les conditions météorologiques restent préoccupantes. Face à la persistance des intempéries et aux risques de glissements de terrain, les autorités ont annoncé la fermeture de tous les établissements scolaires et services publics pour ce mardi 20 octobre, à l’exception des services essentiels.

Dans un communiqué publié ce lundi 19 octobre, le Département de gestion des risques et des catastrophes (DRDM) met en garde contre une forte saturation des sols dans plusieurs régions de l’archipel. De nouvelles précipitations pourraient provoquer des glissements de terrain, des chutes d’arbres et des inondations localisées.

text_a:
More than 180,000 giant tortoises now roam a remote island paradise in the Indian Ocean. Their ancestors came dangerously close to extinction, but decades of conservation have helped turn their survival into one of the most remarkable wildlife recovery stories in the world.

Located in the Seychelles, Aldabra Atoll is home to the world's largest free-roaming population of giant tortoises. These enormous reptiles, scientifically known as Aldabrachelys gigantea, are among the last surviving giant tortoise populations on Earth.

Their history, however, was not always so promising. During the 18th and 19th centuries, sailors and traders heavily exploited giant tortoises for food, often collecting them in large numbers and transporting them aboard ships. By the end of the 19th century, hunting had reduced Aldabra's population to fewer than 1,000 individuals.

Fortunately, stronger conservation measures helped protect the remaining animals and their habitat. Aldabra received strict nature reserve protection in 1981 and was recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.

In October 2026, researchers from the University of Exeter and the Seychelles Islands Foundation announced a new scientific estimate of approximately 182,424 adult and sub-adult tortoises. The research analyzed years of population monitoring data collected between 2018 and 2022.

Interestingly, scientists explained that earlier estimates had probably missed many tortoises hiding in dense vegetation. This means the new figure does not represent a sudden population explosion, but rather a more accurate assessment of how many animals actually live there.

Beyond their impressive numbers, these ancient reptiles play an essential role in their ecosystem. They graze on vegetation, disperse seeds, and influence the growth of plants across the islands, helping maintain the natural balance of their habitat.

Despite their recovery, climate change, prolonged droughts, rising sea levels, and invasive predators continue to threaten their long-term survival.

Aldabra's giant tortoises demonstrate how sustained conservation and scientific monitoring can protect wildlife for generations.

Tanzania - Here we are

Actually it all had started three weeks ago:

All our friends had left Seychelles over the last two months already. With us in Seychelles was only Rene (S/V Phoenix) who’s planning to sail towards the Red Sea some weeks later - otherwise we definitely started feeling lonely.

And we knew we also should start sooner or later as the change of seasons and thus the change of wind direction would arrive within the next few weeks.

Thus we went provisioning on a Monday with the idea to stay a few days at a nice bay in Mahé and start sailing towards East Africa as soon as a suitable weather window appeared. On Tuesday we completed our official check out procedures and said farewell to our agent Vincent, who is a great, friendly, helpful person 🙂

Captain Hubby had kept an eye on the weather forecast and over the last days he had repeatedly mentioned that we might need to leave in a hurry if we wanted to avoid the worst. By Tuesday evening the need to rush was confirmed: the wind at the compression zone caused by the northern tip of Madagascar appeared with 20kts as weak and, much worse, a cyclonic wind rotation just north of the Seychelles became apparent on all three weather forecast models we were monitoring.

So Wednesday morning we raised the anchor and off we went: bye bye Eden island and anchorage, passed Beau Vallon this time without stopping, and headed straight west to exit the Seychelles plateau. Bye Bye freshly cooked veggies, bye bye freshly baked bread: we knew the sea would become rough - but good we had precooked some meals the week before which were waiting in the freezer for us.

Over five days passage was uncomfortable. The forecast had predicted 2m seas with a 8sec period on the beam. That was mostly correct. Thankfully we had deployed the paravanes in time. Thus, with caution, we were able to eat our hot meals and drink coffee without spilling everything.

All in all we can’t complain: we had friends’ boats spilling eggs all over, loosing anchor and chain, loosing life raft,… all caused by the short steep waves of the passage leaving Seychelles.
So our plan had worked out: leaving late in the season and heading towards East Africa instead of Madagascar gave us a somewhat smoother ride 🙂

The sixth day we approached Zanzibar and as we were not keen on a night arrival at our destination, we dared to anchor a short night at the north tip of Zanzibar. Next day early in the morning we continued. And yes, it was good we didn’t sail Pemba channel during night as there were a lot of fishing traps, fishing nets and very tiny fishing boats as soon as we approached the coast.

Having arrived Tanga in the late afternoon Eternaut deserved a proper pressure wash: boobies had left their poo as thank you present for the free ride, keeping them safe during night and the sea had left a salty crust all over the outside.

Check in procedure was completed over the next two days as the billing system for our visa was down a couple times when we visited immigration - other than that all went smooth. 

At this stage we are at anchor in northern Zanzibar and are amazed by the nice beach, the many tourists and that there appear to be even more touts than tourists on the beach. Forget a peaceful stroll on the sand:  “Jambo, Hakuna Matata, No thank you” - you won’t be able to walk 100m without saying these words. And yes, “looking is free” - but we still don’t want to buy your stuff! The touts are much more persistent than in Asia 😞

Last but not least: the cyclonic wind circulation we had spotted on the forecasts three weeks ago really became a tropical depression and drenched Seychelles where there was severe flooding. It is slowly weakening and the remnants should pass east of us tomorrow. If it stays on track we should be nicely protected and, just in case, we deployed our double snubber for the first time ever. Well - at some stage we have to practice our storm anchoring setup :)

text_a:
Researchers just tallied a whopping nearly 183,000 giant tortoises on one remote Seychelles island, an absolute army of them that now outnumbers every single human in the entire country.

Yes, the slow, tank sized reptiles currently have a bigger population than the humans of Seychelles. After being hunted down to fewer than 1,000 in the 1800s, the Aldabra giant tortoises pulled off a comeback so successful that the latest rigorous survey puts the number of adults and near-adults at nearly 183,000. Decades of strict protection (nature reserve since 1981, UNESCO site since 1982) did the heavy lifting. Earlier estimates of 100,000 were basically undercounts because a lot of them were just chilling in the bushes where surveyors couldn’t see them.

The population looks stable, not exploding overnight. They’re still the world’s largest free roaming giant tortoise herd, living on a remote coral atoll basically left alone by people. 

Droughts, rising seas, and invasive rats and cats could still mess things up, but for now the tortoises are quietly winning at the whole “outnumber the locals” thing.

A giant tortoise species that was once nearly wiped out has made an INCREDIBLE comeback, with its population recovering from fewer than 1,000 to approximately 180,000! 🐢❤️

The Aldabra giant tortoise, native to the Seychelles, was driven to the brink of extinction during the 1800s after decades of hunting and exploitation.

At one point, fewer than 1,000 were believed to remain.

But thanks to more than a century of conservation efforts and the protection of their natural habitat, these gentle giants have made an extraordinary recovery.

A new scientific study published in 2026 estimates that nearly 183,000 adult and young adult giant tortoises now live on Aldabra Atoll.

That's more tortoises than the entire human population of the Seychelles!

Researchers say improved survey methods helped reveal just how many of these remarkable animals are thriving across the islands.

Some Aldabra giant tortoises can live for well over 100 years, meaning the species now has a chance to flourish for generations to come.

An incredible reminder of what can happen when humans give nature the protection and time it needs to recover. ❤️🌿 #fblifestyle #education

Justice Ronny Govinden takes Oath as the Court of Appeal Judge

Justice Ronny James Govinden was sworn in as Justice of the Court of Appeal of the Republic of Seychelles this morning during a ceremony held at State House.

The appointment was made by the President of the Republic, Dr Patrick Herminie, pursuant to Article 123 of the Constitution of the Republic of Seychelles, following a proposal by the Constitutional Appointments Authority under Article 122.

During the ceremony, Justice Govinden took two oaths: the Oath of Allegiance to the Constitution and the Judicial Oath, in the presence of the President of the Republic, Dr Patrick Herminie; Vice President, Mr Sebastien Pillay; Speaker of the National Assembly, Ms Azarel Ernesta; Leaders of the National Assembly; and Attorney General, Mr Divino Sabino.

Justice Ronny Govinden assumed office as Chief Justice on 9 November 2020 and led the Supreme Court for almost six years, before resigning from the position on Friday, 6 November 2026.

In a statement issued following the ceremony, Justice Govinden reflected on his tenure as Chief Justice, reaffirming the Judiciary's constitutional responsibility to uphold the rule of law, safeguard judicial independence and ensure the fair and impartial administration of justice.

He further confirmed his commitment to concluding part-heard cases, in accordance with his judicial obligations, while continuing to contribute his experience and expertise to the administration of justice in his new capacity as Justice of the Court of Appeal.

Justice Govinden graduated from the University of Mauritius, where he was awarded an LLB (Hons) degree in 1996. He subsequently completed the Barristers Final Examination Certificate course conducted by the Mauritius Council of Legal Education in 1998. He was called to the Bar of Seychelles as an Attorney-at-Law in 2000.

Also present at the ceremony were Justices of the Court of Appeal, Registrar of the Supreme Court of Seychelles, Ms Juliana Esticot, and Secretary of State for Cabinet Affairs and Head of the Civil Service, Ms Margaret Moumou.

More than 180,000 giant tortoises now roam a remote island paradise in the Indian Ocean. Their ancestors came dangerously close to extinction, but decades of conservation have helped turn their survival into one of the most remarkable wildlife recovery stories in the world.

Located in the Seychelles, Aldabra Atoll is home to the world's largest free-roaming population of giant tortoises. These enormous reptiles, scientifically known as Aldabrachelys gigantea, are among the last surviving giant tortoise populations on Earth.

Their history, however, was not always so promising. During the 18th and 19th centuries, sailors and traders heavily exploited giant tortoises for food, often collecting them in large numbers and transporting them aboard ships. By the end of the 19th century, hunting had reduced Aldabra's population to fewer than 1,000 individuals.

Fortunately, stronger conservation measures helped protect the remaining animals and their habitat. Aldabra received strict nature reserve protection in 1981 and was recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.

In October 2026, researchers from the University of Exeter and the Seychelles Islands Foundation announced a new scientific estimate of approximately 182,424 adult and sub-adult tortoises. The research analyzed years of population monitoring data collected between 2018 and 2022.

Interestingly, scientists explained that earlier estimates had probably missed many tortoises hiding in dense vegetation. This means the new figure does not represent a sudden population explosion, but rather a more accurate assessment of how many animals actually live there.

Beyond their impressive numbers, these ancient reptiles play an essential role in their ecosystem. They graze on vegetation, disperse seeds, and influence the growth of plants across the islands, helping maintain the natural balance of their habitat.

Despite their recovery, climate change, prolonged droughts, rising sea levels, and invasive predators continue to threaten their long-term survival.

Aldabra's giant tortoises demonstrate how sustained conservation and scientific monitoring can protect wildlife for generations.

text_a:
One of the most remarkable wildlife conservation stories comes from the Seychelles, where giant tortoises have recovered from the brink of extinction after more than a century of protection.

In the late 1800s, the population of Aldabra giant tortoises had fallen dramatically, with historical estimates suggesting that only around 1,000 individuals remained.

These enormous reptiles were once widespread across islands in the Indian Ocean. However, centuries of hunting, habitat destruction, and exploitation by sailors caused devastating population declines.

Today, the Aldabra Atoll in Seychelles supports one of the world’s largest populations of giant tortoises, with estimates reaching approximately 100,000 individuals. Higher figures sometimes refer to broader population estimates, but the exact number varies between surveys.

Aldabra is a remote coral atoll that has remained relatively undisturbed by large-scale human development. Its isolation, combined with strict conservation measures, has allowed the tortoises to reproduce and recover naturally.

These animals are among the largest tortoises on Earth. Adult males can weigh more than 200 kilograms, and individuals can survive for well over a century.

Their ecological importance extends beyond their impressive size. Giant tortoises act as ecosystem engineers, grazing vegetation, dispersing seeds, and helping shape the landscapes they inhabit.

As they move across the islands, they influence plant growth and create conditions that support other species.

The Aldabra Atoll was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in recognition of its exceptional biodiversity and ecological importance.

The recovery of these tortoises demonstrates what sustained conservation efforts can achieve when habitats are protected and human pressures are reduced.

At a time when biodiversity loss is accelerating worldwide, their survival offers an important example of how species can recover when given sufficient protection.

🔵 Shaping a Sustainable Future for Seychelles’ Lobster Fishery 🦞 

The Seychelles Fisheries Authority (SFA) in collaboration with The Nature Conservancy's FishPath initiative and supported by the International Climate Initiative, today held a workshop at Savoy Resort and Spa, Beau Vallon, to present and discuss the draft harvest strategy for the lobster fishery.

Bringing together participants from Mahé, Praslin and La Digue, the workshop reviewed the findings of the 2025 lobster stock assessment, current management measures, data collection and proposed rules to guide future fishing activities.

⚠️ The findings raise concerns. The assessment indicates that the lobster stock remains overfished, with large, mature lobsters becoming increasingly rare in surveys and catches.

Participants shared valuable feedback and recommendations, including increasing patrols, strengthening enforcement against illegal fishing, exploring alternative fishing areas and using survey results to help guide the opening of future fishing seasons.

The feedback will help shape the draft harvest strategy, which aims to establish an evidence-based approach to managing the lobster fishery, protecting the resource while safeguarding the livelihoods of licensed fishers.

📊 The stock assessment will be updated using the latest 2026 fisheries data, followed by further engagement with fishers to present the updated findings and finalised strategy.

Sustainable fisheries start with sound science, effective management and collaboration with our fishing communities. 🌊

In 1962, a British journalist bought a tiny, abandoned island in the Indian Ocean for just £8,000.

What he did with it over the next 40 years was extraordinary.

Brendon Grimshaw had been working as a newspaper editor in East Africa when he discovered Moyenne Island, a small patch of land in the Seychelles.

The island had been largely abandoned for decades. Its vegetation was so overgrown that parts of it were almost impossible to walk through.

But Grimshaw saw something worth saving.

He eventually moved there and began an ambitious restoration project with a young Seychellois man named René Antoine Lafortune.

Together, they cleared invasive growth, planted approximately 16,000 trees by hand and created nearly three miles of nature trails.

They also introduced giant tortoises, helping establish a thriving population of the remarkable animals.

Over the years, birds returned, vegetation flourished and the neglected island gradually became a wildlife sanctuary.

As tourism expanded across the Seychelles, Grimshaw reportedly received offers worth millions from people interested in developing the island.

He refused to sell.

Instead, he spent years working toward legal protection for Moyenne.

In 2009, the island was officially designated a national park, securing the future of the place he and Lafortune had spent decades restoring.

Lafortune died in 2007, and Grimshaw followed in 2012 at the age of 87.

Today, Moyenne remains protected, with its forests, walking trails and giant tortoises still welcoming visitors.

He bought an island for £8,000 and left behind a national park. 💛

More than 180,000 giant tortoises now roam a remote island paradise in the Indian Ocean. Their ancestors came dangerously close to extinction, but decades of conservation have helped turn their survival into one of the most remarkable wildlife recovery stories in the world.

Located in the Seychelles, Aldabra Atoll is home to the world's largest free-roaming population of giant tortoises. These enormous reptiles, scientifically known as Aldabrachelys gigantea, are among the last surviving giant tortoise populations on Earth.

Their history, however, was not always so promising. During the 18th and 19th centuries, sailors and traders heavily exploited giant tortoises for food, often collecting them in large numbers and transporting them aboard ships. By the end of the 19th century, hunting had reduced Aldabra's population to fewer than 1,000 individuals.

Fortunately, stronger conservation measures helped protect the remaining animals and their habitat. Aldabra received strict nature reserve protection in 1981 and was recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.

In October 2026, researchers from the University of Exeter and the Seychelles Islands Foundation announced a new scientific estimate of approximately 182,424 adult and sub-adult tortoises. The research analyzed years of population monitoring data collected between 2018 and 2022.

Interestingly, scientists explained that earlier estimates had probably missed many tortoises hiding in dense vegetation. This means the new figure does not represent a sudden population explosion, but rather a more accurate assessment of how many animals actually live there.

Beyond their impressive numbers, these ancient reptiles play an essential role in their ecosystem. They graze on vegetation, disperse seeds, and influence the growth of plants across the islands, helping maintain the natural balance of their habitat.

Despite their recovery, climate change, prolonged droughts, rising sea levels, and invasive predators continue to threaten their long-term survival.

Aldabra's giant tortoises demonstrate how sustained conservation and scientific monitoring can protect wildlife for generations.

Native to Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles, these enormous reptiles live in a protected island ecosystem where their grazing, movement, and seed dispersal help shape the surrounding environment.

For centuries, giant tortoises across the Indian Ocean were heavily exploited by sailors and settlers for food. Hunting and habitat changes caused populations on many islands to disappear, leaving Aldabra as one of the last major strongholds for giant tortoises in the region.

Aldabra’s long-term survival was helped by conservation efforts that protected the atoll from extensive development and exploitation. The site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982, recognizing its exceptional natural value and the importance of preserving its unique wildlife.

A scientific study published in 2026 estimated that approximately 180,000 Aldabra giant tortoises live on Aldabra Atoll. Researchers from the Seychelles Islands Foundation and the University of Exeter contributed to the research, which provides a more comprehensive population estimate than earlier surveys. The tortoises now outnumber the human population of the entire Seychelles nation.

The Aldabra giant tortoise, scientifically known as Aldabrachelys gigantea, is one of the world's largest tortoise species. During the 19th century, intensive hunting for meat and other resources devastated giant tortoise populations across the Indian Ocean, leaving Aldabra as their last major natural stronghold in the region.

By the late 1800s, fewer than 1,000 tortoises may have remained on Aldabra. Conservation efforts gradually reduced human exploitation, allowing the population to recover. The atoll's designation as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982 further strengthened protections for its unique ecosystem.

To produce the new estimate, researchers analyzed tortoise monitoring data collected by field teams between 2018 and 2022. Their statistical models accounted for differences in habitat and the likelihood of tortoises being overlooked during surveys. The study appeared in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution.

The new estimate does not necessarily mean the population nearly doubled in recent decades. Earlier surveys estimated around 100,000 tortoises, but researchers believe those methods may have missed animals hidden in dense vegetation or shaded areas. The latest research provides a more reliable picture of a population that appears to have remained relatively stable during the study period.

Aldabra's giant tortoises also play an important ecological role. As large herbivores, they graze on vegetation, create pathways through the landscape, and disperse seeds. These activities help shape the atoll's habitats and influence the other species living there.

Despite their impressive numbers, the tortoises remain vulnerable because their principal wild population is concentrated on one remote atoll. Climate change, rising sea levels, and extreme weather could threaten their habitat in the future. Continued monitoring and conservation management will be important to protect the population.

The discovery demonstrates the value of long-term habitat protection and improved scientific monitoring. Aldabra's giant tortoises have survived centuries of human exploitation, and the latest research shows how sustained conservation can help preserve one of the world's most extraordinary wildlife populations.

🇸🇨 **Seychelles counts **[**record number of giant tortoises**](https://afrinz.ru/en/2026/10/seychelles-counts-record-number-of-giant-tortoises/) 

About 183,000 giant tortoises live on Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles — this is the highest population estimate in the history of observations, reports the Seychelles Nation, citing an international study.

🔸Scientists from the Seychelles Islands Foundation and the University of Exeter in the UK analysed observation data collected on Aldabra between 2018 and 2022, and the results of their work were published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution. According to the researchers’ estimates, the population of giant tortoises on the atoll remains stable. Thus, Aldabra is home to the world’s largest population of these animals living in the wild.

🔸Previously, the Aldabra tortoise population was estimated at approximately 100,000 individuals. However, the scientists note that this does not indicate a sharp increase in the population over the past decades. The researchers hypothesize that previous counting methods failed to detect many tortoises that were hidden in the atoll’s dense vegetation.

🔸Scientists also noted that the situation is particularly significant in the context of Aldabra’s history. In the 19th century, due to mass hunting, the population of giant tortoises there dwindled to fewer than 1,000 individuals. Today, the atoll is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and remains one of the most important natural sites in the Seychelles.

THE LIGHTHOUSE DOESN'T BELONG TO THE KEEPER
OracleMaster  Reflection :

On 6 November 2026, the Office of the President announced the resignation of Chief Justice Rony Govinden. A chapter has closed at the highest level of Seychelles' judiciary.

But the question isn't simply who comes next. The more important question is:

What do we want justice to look like moving forward?

THE LIGHTHOUSE PRINCIPLE

A lighthouse doesn't exist to honour its keeper. It exists so that every ship can trust the light it provides.

When a lighthouse keeper steps down, a wise harbour doesn't simply hand over the keys to the next person. It inspects the lamp, cleans the glass and asks whether the light remains trustworthy.

Chief Justice Govinden's resignation presents Seychelles with precisely that opportunity.

The strength of a judiciary isn't measured by the names displayed on its doors, but by the confidence the public places in its independence, integrity and impartiality.

🌱 WHY THIS MOMENT IS AN OPPORTUNITY

✨ An opportunity to reset standards, not merely change personnel.

✨ An opportunity to strengthen the systems that safeguard fairness and accountability.

✨ A reminder that no individual officeholder is greater than the institution they serve.

A resignation should not become a revolving door. Mr Govinden's departure could instead become a doorway to institutional renewal.

 THE CORE MESSAGE

1. Transparency over assumptions.

Concerns raised over the years deserve independent scrutiny. They should neither be buried nor presented as established facts without proper investigation.

2. Institutions over individuals.

There has been public discussion about whether Mr Govinden might seek another judicial appointment, such as Justice of Appeal. Any such appointment should be examined against the principles of public confidence, institutional integrity and judicial independence.

3. Impartiality must not only exist; it must be seen.

Even where no wrongdoing has been established, the justice system must maintain public confidence. Potential conflicts of interest and even the appearance of undue influence must be carefully addressed.

4. Accountability applies to everyone.

Oversight bodies and the Constitutional Appointments Authority must be prepared to face the same level of scrutiny they are expected to apply to others.

THE VISION

Imagine a Seychelles where every judicial appointment is open to scrutiny, where oversight institutions act with courage and independence, and where citizens can proudly say:

"Our courts belong to the people."

This is not about condemning anyone without evidence. It is about demanding transparency, independent review and the highest standards of public accountability.

The departure of a Chief Justice should mark the beginning of a new chapter, not simply the recycling of leadership while legitimate questions remain unanswered.

That's not a dream. That's a decision.

 The initiative, which was officially launched this week, introduces dedicated sorting bins where residents can bring selected recyclable materials for collection and onward processing by local recyclers.

The aim is to recover valuable materials, reduce the amount of waste sent to landfill, and make recycling more accessible to communities.

♻️ What can residents recycle at the centre?

The designated bins are intended for the collection of:

- 🔋 Batteries
- ♻️ Selected types of plastics, including PET plastic bottles
- 🔩 Metals
- 💻 Electronic waste (e-waste)
- 🥫 Aluminium and other cans
- 🍾 Glass drinking bottles

The initiative is co-led by the ISLANDS Project (UNDP Seychelles) and IslandPlas Project (IUCN) in collaboration with the Ministry of Environment, Climate, Energy and Natural Resources (#mecenr), the Landscape and Waste Management Agency (LWMA).
It is supported by local recycling partners: Metaluco, Brikole, Precious Plastic and DeRecycler, who play an important role in ensuring that collected materials can be recovered and put to further use.

🌱 A shared responsibility

The launch of SCRI in Anse Aux Pins is a starting point for bringing recycling closer to residents and encouraging more responsible waste-management practices. Its success will depend on community participation and the proper separation of recyclable materials.
Residents are encouraged to make use of the facility and help keep valuable resources out of our landfill.
